title: Partitioning
summary: How to break a large dataset into partitions (shards) spread across many nodes for scalability, how to choose a partitioning scheme, keep it balanced as the cluster grows, and route requests to the right partition.
keyTakeaways: Partitioning spreads data and query load across nodes for scalability; it is normally combined with replication so each partition has copies.
Key-range partitioning keeps keys sorted (enabling range scans) but risks hot spots; hash partitioning spreads load evenly but loses efficient range queries.
Even hashing does not fix a single hot key; that needs application-level splitting such as appending a random suffix.
Secondary indexes are either document-partitioned (local, scatter/gather reads) or term-partitioned (global, writes fan out but reads hit one partition).
Rebalancing should avoid hash-mod-N; fixed-partition-count, dynamic split/merge, and per-node-proportional strategies move data without reshuffling everything.
Request routing (node forwarding, a routing tier, or a partition-aware client) needs consensus on partition assignments — often via ZooKeeper or a gossip protocol.

questions.q: In DDIA, what is the main goal of partitioning (sharding)?
options: To keep multiple copies of the same data for fault tolerance
To guarantee transactions execute in a serial order
To spread data and query load across many nodes so the system scales beyond one machine
To compress data by removing duplicate rows
questions.explain: Partitioning splits a large dataset so different nodes hold different subsets, scaling storage and throughput. Keeping copies for fault tolerance is replication — the two are usually combined but are distinct concerns.

questions.q: What does it mean for a partitioning scheme to be 'skewed', and why is it bad?
options: Partitions are unevenly loaded so some nodes ('hot spots') get disproportionate data or traffic, undermining the scalability partitioning was meant to provide
Data is sorted incorrectly, breaking range queries
Replicas of a partition disagree on the current value
The partition key is stored in a different byte order than the sort key
questions.explain: Skew means load isn't spread evenly; hot spots bottleneck on a few nodes while others idle. The goal of a good scheme is even distribution across partitions.

questions.q: What is the key tradeoff of partitioning by key range (keys kept sorted within each partition)?
options: It distributes load perfectly evenly but makes point lookups slow
It loses the ability to do point lookups entirely
It requires rehashing all data whenever a node is added
It enables efficient range scans, but certain access patterns (e.g., a timestamp key) can create hot spots
questions.explain: Sorted key ranges support range queries, but a key like a timestamp funnels all recent writes into one partition, creating a hot spot. Even distribution is the strength of hash partitioning, not key-range.

questions.q: What does partitioning by hash of the key gain and lose compared to key-range partitioning?
options: Gains efficient range queries, loses even distribution
Gains even load distribution, loses efficient range queries (adjacent keys scatter across partitions)
Gains both range queries and even distribution with no downside
Gains stronger consistency, loses availability
questions.explain: Hashing spreads keys uniformly (good for load) but destroys key adjacency, so a range scan must query every partition. Key-range partitioning is the opposite tradeoff.

questions.q: How does Cassandra's compound primary key compromise between hash and range partitioning?
options: It hashes every column of the key together into one partition ID
It stores each column in a separate partition
It hashes the first part of the key to choose a partition, then keeps rows sorted by the remaining columns within that partition
It uses consistent hashing across all key columns
questions.explain: The first column of a Cassandra compound key is hashed to pick the partition (even spread), while the remaining columns sort rows inside the partition (efficient range scans within one partition key). This gives one-partition range queries without global hot spots.

questions.q: Why does hash partitioning fail to solve the problem of a single hot key (e.g., a celebrity's user ID getting huge traffic)?
options: All requests for one key still hash to the same single partition, so hashing can't split load for an individual key
Hashing makes the hot key even hotter by duplicating it
Hashing only distributes writes, not reads
Hash functions are too slow to keep up with a hot key
questions.explain: A hash spreads different keys evenly, but every request for the same key lands on one partition — a single hot key stays on one node. The book's mitigation is application-level: e.g., append a random number to the key to split it across N partitions, at the cost of more complex reads.

questions.q: How does a document-partitioned (local) secondary index behave on reads?
options: A single partition holds the whole index, so reads hit exactly one partition
Reads never use the index; they scan primary keys
The index is stored on the client, so no partition is queried
Each partition indexes only its own documents, so a query on the secondary index must scatter to all partitions and gather results
questions.explain: A local (document-partitioned) index keeps each partition's index alongside its own data, so a secondary-index query fans out to every partition (scatter/gather). Writes stay local — the opposite tradeoff from a global/term-partitioned index.

questions.q: What is the tradeoff of a term-partitioned (global) secondary index versus a local one?
options: Reads must query all partitions, but writes touch only one
Reads hit a single partition (fast), but a write may need to update index entries on several partitions
Both reads and writes always touch exactly one partition
It eliminates the need to store a primary index
questions.explain: A global index is partitioned by the indexed term, so a read on that term hits one partition — but a single document write can affect several terms living on different partitions, making writes fan out (and often asynchronous). This is the mirror image of the local-index tradeoff.

questions.q: Why should rebalancing NOT be done with 'hash mod N' (where N is the number of nodes)?
options: Modulo is too computationally expensive at scale
Modulo produces collisions that corrupt keys
Changing N reassigns most keys to different nodes, forcing an enormous, disruptive data movement
It only works when N is a power of two
questions.explain: With `hash mod N`, adding or removing a node changes N and remaps almost every key, so nearly all data must move. Rebalancing strategies aim to move as little data as possible.

questions.q: How does the 'fixed number of partitions' rebalancing strategy work?
options: It creates many more partitions than nodes up front and, when nodes are added, moves whole partitions between nodes without changing how keys map to partitions
It picks the partition count equal to the current node count and re-splits on every change
It splits a partition in two whenever it exceeds a size threshold
It uses hash mod N but caches the result
questions.explain: You over-provision partitions (e.g., 1000 for 10 nodes) so rebalancing just reassigns entire partitions to new nodes; the key→partition mapping never changes. Splitting on a size threshold is the separate 'dynamic partitioning' strategy (HBase/B-trees).

questions.q: What characterizes 'dynamic partitioning' as used by HBase and range-partitioned stores?
options: The number of partitions is fixed forever at cluster creation
Partitions are reassigned every time a client connects
Each node always holds exactly one partition
Partitions are split when they grow too large and merged when they shrink, so partition count adapts to the data volume — analogous to a B-tree
questions.explain: Dynamic partitioning splits an overgrown partition and merges under-filled ones, letting the number of partitions track the dataset size (like B-tree node splits/merges). Fixed-count is the alternative where partition count never changes.

questions.q: Which three approaches to request routing does DDIA describe?
options: Only client-side routing is possible in distributed databases
A node receives the request and forwards it; a routing tier decides and forwards; or a partition-aware client connects directly to the right node
DNS round-robin, load balancer, and reverse proxy
Leader forwarding, follower forwarding, and quorum voting
questions.explain: The three models are: any node forwards to the owner, a dedicated routing tier acts as a partition-aware load balancer, or the client itself knows the partition assignment. All three need current knowledge of which partition lives on which node.

questions.q: What role does ZooKeeper commonly play in a partitioned system's request routing?
options: It stores the actual partitioned data as a backup
It hashes keys to partitions on behalf of clients
It maintains authoritative metadata about partition-to-node assignments, and routing components subscribe to it for changes
It executes the parallel query plan across partitions
questions.explain: ZooKeeper acts as the coordination service holding the authoritative mapping of partitions to nodes; routing tiers/clients watch it so they learn about rebalancing. A gossip protocol among the nodes is the decentralized alternative that avoids a separate coordinator.

questions.q: What is massively parallel processing (MPP) in the context of partitioning?
options: Running the same query on every replica and voting on the result
A routing scheme that picks the least-loaded node
A replication topology for multi-datacenter writes
Breaking a complex analytic query into stages that execute in parallel across many partitions/nodes to speed up throughput-heavy workloads
questions.explain: MPP query engines parallelize a single analytic query across the partitions/nodes holding the data, which suits scan-heavy analytics rather than the point queries typical of OLTP. It is about query execution, not replication or routing.
